snip.t: Social: education, alcohol, smoking, drugs, occupation (radiation, halothane, chemical exposure) and income (low socio-economic status is linked to pre-eclampsia and preterm labour).
Weight: A gain of more than 1 kg a week is abnormal (fluid retention, pre-eclampsia)
Blood pressure: Falls early; the diastolic falls more (up to 15 mmHg); lowest at 24–28 weeks; rises towards term but not above pre-pregnancy values — A raised BP is never normal: think pre-eclampsia
BP of 130/80 or more in the second trimester is not "normal for pregnancy": check urine protein and think pre-eclampsia.
A gravida 6 para 4+1 admitted with severe pre-eclampsia.

snip.t: Severe pre-eclampsia with a symptom: control BP, give magnesium sulphate, give antenatal steroids for fetal lungs, then deliver within 24 to 48 hours.

ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: Eclampsia is new-onset generalized seizures in a woman with pre‑eclampsia, occurring before, during, or after delivery. It signals life‑threatening cerebral involvement and requires immediate stabilization and delivery.

sections.p: Eclampsia is diagnosed when a pregnant or postpartum woman with pre‑eclampsia (BP ≥140/90 mmHg after 20 wks + proteinuria or other end‑organ signs) develops unexplained tonic‑clonic seizures.
b: Seizure must not be explained by epilepsy, infection, or metabolic disturbance

t.b: Is hypertension present? If ≥140/90 mmHg, supports pre‑eclampsia diagnosis

sections.p: Pre‑eclampsia severity guides urgency: severe features include BP ≥160/110 mmHg, platelets <100 000, creatinine >1.1 mg/dL, liver enzymes ≥2× ULN, pulmonary edema, or neurologic symptoms.
b: Severe disease demands delivery within 24‑48 h and magnesium sulfate

t.b: Is thrombocytopenia present? <100 000 indicates severe disease
Is renal function impaired? >1.1 mg/dL signals severe disease

sections.p: Eclampsia arises from abnormal placental perfusion leading to systemic endothelial dysfunction. Risk factors (most common first) include nulliparity, pre‑existing hypertension, diabetes, obesity, low socioeconomic status, and chronic kidney disease. In low‑resource settings add malaria, HIV, and use of herbal vasoconstrictors.
b: Placental ischemia is the primary pathophysiologic trigger

sections.p: Typical presentation: sudden generalized tonic‑clonic seizure in a woman with hypertension, headache, visual disturbances, epigastric pain, or edema. Post‑ictal confusion is common.
b: Look for preceding headache, visual changes, or right upper quadrant pain

sections.p: Investigations confirm severity, exclude mimics, and guide management. When a test is unavailable, rely on clinical signs and bedside tools.

t.b: Is magnesium level therapeutic? >2 mmol/L after loading indicates adequate prophylaxis
Are transaminases >2× ULN? Suggests severe disease
Is fetal distress present? Non‑reassuring pattern mandates delivery

sections.p: Immediate threats: status epilepticus, pulmonary edema, intracerebral hemorrhage, HELLP syndrome, DIC, and placental abruption. Maternal mortality rises with delayed seizure control or uncontrolled hypertension.
b: Any recurrent seizure after magnesium is a red flag

sections.p: Stabilize airway, breathing, circulation; give magnesium sulfate IV (loading then maintenance) to prevent further seizures; control BP with labetalol or hydralazine; give corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity if <34 wks; plan delivery—usually vaginal induction or cesarean if obstetric urgency.
b: Magnesium stops seizures; antihypertensives prevent further cerebral injury

sections.p: After delivery, monitor BP and magnesium levels for 24‑48 h; continue antihypertensives until normotensive for 6 weeks. Counsel on future pregnancy risk (≈20% recurrence) and advise low‑dose aspirin prophylaxis in subsequent pregnancies.
Conditions that mimic eclampsia include epilepsy, cerebral malaria, meningitis, severe hypoglycemia, and hypertensive encephalopathy without proteinuria.
b: Check glucose and malaria smear in endemic areas

sections.p: Proteinuria may be absent in severe pre‑eclampsia; normal platelet count does not exclude severe disease if other organ dysfunction exists. In malaria‑endemic zones, cerebral malaria can present with seizures and hypertension, misleading diagnosis.
b: Do not rely on a single lab value

whenToSeekHelp: New seizure in pregnancy, persistent hypertension >160/110 mmHg, severe headache or visual loss, epigastric pain, decreased urine output, sudden shortness of breath

faq.q: Why does magnesium sulfate stop seizures?
faq.a: It stabilizes neuronal membranes and reduces NMDA‑mediated excitatory transmission.
Yes, up to 48 h after delivery; vigilance continues after birth.
Delivery removes the placenta, the source of endothelial injury, and resolves the disease.
